notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 89:1–26, drawn only from pages I actually read. Some limits first:
- **Missing or thin sources.** I found nothing from an Orthodox site, nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching, and no bibleodyssey.org page. Verses 16–17 and 22–25 got fewer comments.
- **Cut-off pages.** The Enduring Word page I opened stopped at v. 15, and the NET notes I opened stop at the v. 14 note. Kingcomments, a dispensational commentary on StudyLight, stops partway through v. 21.
- **Citations.** Points from those three opened pages have a URL but no quotation tags.
- **Little real Protestant disagreement.** Most Protestant writers agree. Where they differ, it is mainly over how directly a verse speaks of Christ, and over v. 19 and v. 26. I've labelled each writer's tradition only where the page itself shows it.

**Title / v. 1**
- Ethan is the wise man named in 1 Kings 4:31, praised for wisdom but outdone by Solomon. So he probably lived under both Solomon and David. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
- Spurgeon (Baptist) thinks he may be the same man as Jeduthun. If so, he must have written this Psalm in his old age, when troubles were coming thick and heavy upon the dynasty of David. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps089.cfm
- Guzik: "mercies" translates *hesed*, God's loyal covenant love. The psalm is full of trouble, yet the trouble does not stop the praise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
- Barnes: God made David king purely out of mercy, because he was not in the royal line, and had no claim to the crown. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-1.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** he reads the title as pointing to Christ himself. He says the name Ethan means "strong", and that no one is strong except by hoping in God's promises. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801089.htm

**v. 2**
- Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "built up" echoes 2 Samuel 7, where David wants to build God a house and God promises to build David a house instead. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
- Kingcomments: God's faithfulness is as fixed as the sun, moon and stars in the sky. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-89.html
- NET note: "you set up your faithfulness" may picture God's heavenly throne, from which he makes his unconditional promises. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=89
- **Augustine:** God's truth in keeping his promises could not be shown unless mercy in the remission of sins preceded. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801089.htm

**vv. 3–4**
- Spurgeon: God's own words here sum up the original covenant of 2 Samuel 7, made with David and sealed with an oath. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps089.cfm
- Guzik: Solomon fulfilled the promise in part. Jesus, the Son of David, fulfils it completely. "Selah" calls for a pause to think about the promise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
- Kingcomments: God alone takes on all the obligations of this covenant, with no conditions attached. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-89.html
- NET note: the speaker changes. God speaks in vv. 3–4, the psalmist in vv. 1–2. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=89
- **Augustine:** the covenant meant is the new one, and David's seed is Christ (Galatians 3:16). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801089.htm

**v. 5**
- Who are the "holy ones"?
  - Guzik: several commentators take them to be angels. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
  - Coffman disagrees: "This is a frequent term in the Old Testament as a reference to Israel as God's Old Testament church." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-10.html
  - Kingcomments thinks of God's people gathered on earth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-89.html
- Spurgeon links the verse to the angels' song at Bethlehem. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps089.cfm
- **Modern scholarship (NET):** "holy ones" can mean God's people, but here it refers to God's heavenly assembly and the angels that surround his throne. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=89
- **Catholic (Haydock):** the heavens, meaning the angels, praise God fittingly. He adds Augustine's point that preachers announce the same praise in the Church. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/psalms-88.html

**vv. 6–8**
- Guzik: that no one compares with God is part of what "holy" means. "Holy" means set apart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
- Kingcomments: God is not just the leader of a circle of angels. He is their Creator, and "God of Hosts" means every power is under him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-89.html
- **NET:** "sons of gods" appears only here and in Psalm 29:1. In Canaanite texts the high god El's council was called "the sons of El", and the heavenly assembly (comprised of so-called "angels" and other supernatural beings) appears to be in view. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=89
- Bible.org (Utley) also reads vv. 5–8 as God leading the angelic council. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-89

**vv. 9–10**
- Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: calming the sea and breaking Egypt show God's almighty power. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
- Wesley (Methodist) says simply: Rhahab — Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-10.html
- Ellicott: the sea reminded the poet of the Red Sea, with Egypt represented as some huge monster conquered and crushed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-10.html
- Guzik on the Canaanite background:
  - "Rahab" means "proud one". In Canaanite myth the sea and a sea serpent were defeated at creation. The Bible takes this picture over and reshapes it to honour Yahweh alone.
  - He also allows that Rahab could be a form of Satan.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
- Kingcomments: Rahab is Egypt, shown so as to reveal the evil power behind it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-89.html
- **NET:** it could point back to the Exodus. But because Rahab is linked with the sea here, the name probably works as a symbol, perhaps recalling creation, when God overcame the deep and brought order out of chaos. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=89 Utley lists both the chaos monster and Egypt as possible meanings. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-89

**vv. 11–12**
- Guzik: no other god made or keeps up heaven and earth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
- Kingcomments:
  - Tabor lies west of the Jordan and Hermon to the east, so together with north and south they cover all four directions.
  - The earth seems not to be God's right now because of sin, yet faith still says "the earth is Yours".
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-89.html
- NET: Tabor and Hermon were two of the most prominent mountains in Palestine. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=89

**v. 13**
- Guzik: we can see God's arm even more clearly in Jesus' death and resurrection. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
- NET: arm, hand and right hand stand for God's actions, especially his victories in war. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=89

**v. 14**
- Clarke, quoted by Guzik: mercy and truth are like heralds announcing the Judge's arrival. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
- Kingcomments: in God, absolute power goes together with absolute justice, so he needs no "separation of powers". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-89.html
- **Augustine:** he would fear God's judgment seat if mercy and truth did not go before God, wiping out sins and keeping promises. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801089.htm

**v. 15**
- Maclaren: "joyful sound" is the technical word for the trumpet blast at Jewish feasts. He says it does not refer to gospel preaching. The light of God's face means his favour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-15.htm
- Matthew Henry (Presbyterian) applies it to the gospel: The gospel is indeed a joyful sound, a sound of victory, of liberty, of communion with God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_089.cfm
- Clarke connects it to the jubilee trumpet that proclaimed freedom for captives. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-15.html
- Calvin (Reformed): walking in God's light means trusting his providence, sure that he truly cares for our good. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-15.html
- Gill (Baptist) adds that believers walk in this sunshine though not always; for sometimes they walk in darkness. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/asv/psalms/89-15.html
- Kingcomments (dispensational): it recalls the Feast of Trumpets, pictures Israel's future restoration, and points to the millennium. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-89.html
- NET renders the verse: How blessed are the people who worship you! https://biblehub.com/lexicon/psalms/89-15.htm

**vv. 16–17**
- Calvin: "rejoicing in His name" and "glorying in His righteousness" mean the same thing as walking in His light. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-15.html
- Matthew Henry (Concise): Though believers are nothing in themselves, yet having all in Christ Jesus, they may rejoice in his name. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-15.htm
- Kingcomments: the "horn" is a picture of strength. Being lifted up is God's free gift of grace, not something earned. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-89.html
- NET translates v. 16b as "vindicated by your justice" and v. 17b as "we are victorious". https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=89

**v. 18**
- Kingcomments: the "shield" and "king" are the Messiah, given to Israel by the Holy One of Israel. Isaiah uses "Holy One of Israel" as a title for God 25 times. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-89.html

**v. 19**
- Who received the vision?
  - Matthew Henry: the promise was spoken in vision to Nathan the prophet, 2 Samuel 7:12-17. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-26.html
  - Kingcomments thinks it may have been Samuel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-89.html
- Clarke on the text: many manuscripts read the plural, "holy ones". https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-19.html
- Calvin translates "meek ones" and stresses that God chose the king; he was not elected by people and did not seize power. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-19.html
- Spurgeon applies "chosen from the people" to Christ's humble birth and real humanity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-19.html

**v. 20**
- Matthew Henry (Concise): the anointing is a picture of Christ, the King, Priest and Prophet anointed with the Holy Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-26.htm
- Kingcomments: David was already God's servant while keeping sheep. For believers, the anointing stands for the Holy Spirit (1 John 2:20). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-89.html
- **Augustine** links this verse to Psalm 45's "oil of gladness above your fellows", which he applies to Christ. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801089.htm

**v. 21**
- Kingcomments: God promises that David's service will succeed, the same hand and arm as in v. 13. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-89.html

**vv. 22–23**
- Matthew Henry (Concise): David after his anointing, was persecuted, but none could gain advantage against him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-26.htm

**v. 24**
- **Augustine:**
  - God showed us mercy (forgiving sins) and truth (keeping promises), so we should give mercy and truth back to him: mercy toward the wretched, truth in judging fairly.
  - On the horn lifted up, he says: You are Christians, recognise Christ.
  - https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801089.htm
- Smith: the horn stands for strength, so God's name will be David's strength. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-19.html

**v. 25**
- Matthew Henry: it is in the kingdom of the Messiah that this has its full accomplishment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_089.cfm

**v. 26**
- This is where the Protestant writers differ most.
- Calvin (Reformed): this king's chief honour is being counted God's son. Kings and believers are also called sons, but David is raised above them all. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-26.html
- Gill (Baptist) reads it of Christ alone. God is "Father" here not by adoption, as he is the Father of saints; but by generation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-26.html
- Matthew Henry hears Christ's own prayers in this verse ("Father, forgive them"). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-26.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary quotes Molyneux: the verse is unintelligible in reference to David. It adds that every believer may now call God Father. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-26.html
- Ellicott (Anglican) sees it as a clue to the psalm's date. "Father" is a title for the Divine Being which the national religion did not frame till the exile period. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-26.html
- Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary root it in 2 Samuel 7:14 and 22:2–3, 47: the king relies on God as his only hope. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-26.htm
